newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia agrees debt deal with London Club creditors.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia agrees debt deal with London Club creditors.

text.p: Bosnian government officials on Tuesday celebrated a last-minute agreement with the London Club of commercial bank creditors to restructure its $1.04 billion debt.
Bosnia began negotiations with the club last Wednesday in London and clinched a deal late on Monday night just before a deadline which was due to expire at midnight.

"This is a great step towards normalisation of our relationship with financial institutions and it opens the way for new arrangements and new credits," Bosnia's co-prime minister Haris Silajdzic told reporters.
Bosnia assumed responsibility for servicing $404 million of the $1.04 billion debt, said Hasan Muratovic, the country's minister of economy and foreign trade.
The rest has either been taken over by other former Yugoslav republics or has been written off.
Of the $404 million, $254 million will have to be paid only when the country reaches a set level of Gross Domestic Product, Muratovic said.
The remaining $150 million is to be paid in 20 years with a seven-year grace period.
Muratovic said Bosnia will pay annual interest of two percent in the first five years, rising to three percent in the following three years and 3.5 percent in the next two years.
"We shall start paying the principal off after the seventh year in 26 semi-annual instalments at an interest rate based on Libor (London Interbank Offered Rate) plus 0.825 percent," he said.
Muratovic said repayment of the $254 million amount would begin only after Bosnia's GDP per capita level rose to $2,800, indexed to German inflation from 1997, and stayed there for two years.
It will be paid in 24 instalments at the same Libor interest rate plus 0.825 percent, he said.
As part of the agreement, Bosnia would issue its first peacetime bonds denominated in German marks listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.
The bonds initially would be issued only for the $150 million amount, with performance bonds to follow when the country begins servicing the remaining $254 million, Muratovic said.

Many creditors have already written off Bosnia's debt due to the war which began in 1991 following disintegration of the old Yugoslav federation. Since then, the former republics have had to negotiate their share of its huge debt.
In June 1996, the London club issued Bosnia with a one year waiver requiring it to reach an agreement by midnight (2200 GMT) on Monday.

If the deadline had expired without a deal, Bosnia would have faced much more difficult conditions. Present-day Yugoslavia, now composed only of Serbia and Montenegro, would have been allowed to enter the negotiations.
Yugoslavia has bought a major stake in the debt and could have blocked any future deal with the London club, foreign experts said.
